prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene, opening moire flat-band quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene has a rare combination of a simple, quantitative theoretical idea (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, in which a single twist angle quenches the kinetic energy and makes interactions dominate) and a decisive experimental realisation in 2018 that showed correlated insulators and superconductivity. Seen from statistical physics, the twist angle is a new control parameter for tuning the ratio of interaction to bandwidth, and this has seeded a broad family of moire platforms with correlated, superconducting and topological phases. The theory-plus-experiment attribution is separable and fits three names. Independent confirmation across many laboratories since 2018 makes the phenomenology robust, and the field is large and still productive, so recognition is timely.
statement.case_against: The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is still unresolved, and sample-to-sample variability remains a practical problem, so the prize would honour a platform and its phenomenology rather than a settled microscopic explanation. Attribution is also incomplete: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, is outside the credited names, and other groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others) contributed major later results. Eight years is short compared with the typical Nobel lag, and it risks looking premature next to candidates with decades of confirmed impact such as B030 or B024.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator candidate (B030) first as one of the strongest cases: original, conceptually clear, and spread across condensed matter, photonics and materials, with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I agree B030 is conceptually deep and mature, and I keep it as my first alternative. But my reservation is attribution, not merit: with Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Molenkamp, Konig and Hasan all with legitimate claims, any three names will leave out someone with a strong case, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases of matter. Twisted bilayer graphene has a much cleaner prediction-plus-discovery split, so I consider it the more defensible configuration despite its youth.

responses.point: Kroll puts the optical lattice clock (B024, Katori and Ye) first as the clearest advance in measurement accuracy, with a clean two-name credit and consequences for geodesy, fundamental-constant tests and a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution for B024 is cleaner than for almost anything else on the list and that the 10^-18 result is solid and mature, which is why I list it as a second alternative. I do not agree that clarity of credit alone should decide it. The clocks refine an established line of precision spectroscopy, while twisted bilayer graphene created an entirely new class of tunable many-body states and a research field. I would be less opposed to B024 as a second part of a shared prize than as the sole prize, but I would still place the conceptual novelty of moire flat bands higher.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B002) first and trapped ions (B006) second, arguing that circuit QED is the architecture of essentially every superconducting processor and that the quantum-information platforms are the best-established routes to computation.
responses.response: The technological importance of circuit QED is not in doubt, but I am hesitant for two reasons. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits lies directly upstream, and the four-way credit (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) forces an arbitrary exclusion of Girvin or Blais. I would also not equate platform importance for quantum computing with a fundamental physics discovery; twisted bilayer graphene delivers new states of matter. I remain open to B002 if the committee wants a quantum-information theme, but I would not rank it above B021.

responses.point: Olsson also ranks twisted bilayer graphene first but proposes only two laureates, MacDonald for theory and Jarillo-Herrero for experiment, treating Bistritzer's role as a real but secondary allocation.
responses.response: I take the two-name option seriously, since it keeps the prize tight. But Bistritzer was first author on the 2011 paper that derived the magic angle and the flat bands, so omitting him would cut away the very result that defines the prediction. Since the three-person limit is not binding here and none of the other claimants is in the credited list, I prefer including all three. The harder question, which Olsson does not resolve, is Yuan Cao, who is not credited and whom I flag as an unresolved attribution issue.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B021 first as a theory-led discovery with clearly separable prediction and first experimental demonstrations, but notes that early moire band-structure work and independent experimental groups are omitted from the credit.
responses.response: I agree with the framing of a theory-led discovery. On the omitted early moire band-structure work and independent groups, I think the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction is distinctly the quantitative origin of the magic angle, and the independent confirmations strengthen maturity rather than dilute attribution. Eriksson's second choice, TMR (B005), has by contrast an acknowledged uncredited parallel MgO contribution, which makes its attribution weaker than that of B021.

uncertainties: Whether the superconducting mechanism remaining unresolved makes a prize at eight years too early.
Whether Yuan Cao and other early experimental contributors should displace or accompany one of the three credited names.

Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize pairing a condensed-matter achievement with a precision or quantum-information achievement (for example B024 or B030), which I have not fully resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. Mehlig's documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include any credited person on the shortlist.
